extracted.intended_audience: students, philosophers, scientists, and practitioners interested in logic and the methods of scientific investigation
extracted.subtask_description: A classic treatise (John Stuart Mill) setting out the principles of evidence, rules of reasoning (induction and deduction), and the methods of scientific investigation, aimed at guiding how to judge and produce proofs and laws. It combines analytic accounts of inference with practical canons for observation, experiment, classification, and avoidance of fallacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logic defined as the science of operations for pursuing truth
rubrics_metrics.description: "Logic is the science which treats of the operations of the human understanding in the pursuit of truth."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill states the central aim of logic: to analyse intellectual operations that facilitate the estimation of evidence. This definition anchors subsequent criteria: logic's job is to supply canons for testing the sufficiency of evidence to prove a proposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logic as the science of Proof or Evidence (not of Belief or Intuition)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The province of logic must be restricted to that portion of our knowledge which consists of inferences from truths previously known; ... Logic is not the science of Belief, but the science of Proof, or Evidence."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between truths known by immediate consciousness (intuition) and truths known by inference; logic concerns only the latter. Questions about what is primitive (intuition, consciousness) belong to metaphysics, not logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasoning includes both induction and deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Mill adopts a wide sense of 'reasoning': "to reason is simply to infer any assertion, from assertions already admitted: and in this sense, induction is as much entitled to be called reasoning as the demonstrations of geometry."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations of arguments must treat inductive inferences and deductive/syllogistic inferences under the same logical standards of evidence and correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operations subsidiary to inference (naming, definition, classification)
rubrics_metrics.description: "It includes, therefore, the operation of Naming; for language is an instrument of thought... It includes, also, Definition, and Classification."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precision in naming, sound principles of definition, and correct classification are instrumental to making evidence accessible and to judging it correctly. These are part of logic's remit because they facilitate inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit of logical analysis — analyse only as far as needed to expose error
rubrics_metrics.description: Mill: the analysis of reasoning should go "so far only as may be requisite for ascertaining the difference between a correct and an incorrect performance of those processes."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not demand ultimate psychological decomposition; logic's analysis is practical and needs only to the point where incorrectness in inference becomes detectable for the purposes of the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logician's role: judge of sufficiency of evidence, not discoverer of facts
rubrics_metrics.description: "Logic neither observes, nor invents, nor discovers; but judges. It is no part of the business of logic to inform the surgeon what appearances are found... But logic sits in judgment on the sufficiency of that observation and experience to justify his rules..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating scientific work, apply logical tests to determine whether available data can legitimately be taken to prove the claimed conclusions; do not expect logic to supply the empirical observations themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility requirement: logic must be useful to be genuine science
rubrics_metrics.description: "If a science of logic exists, or is capable of existing, it must be useful. ... there are limits both to what mechanicians can do without principles of mechanics, and to what thinkers can do without principles of logic."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules of logic should improve the practice of inquiry; criteria should be judged by their effectiveness in enabling correct inferences across scientific disciplines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between intuitive (consciousness) knowledge and inferential knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: "Truths are known to us in two ways: some are known directly, and of themselves; some through the medium of other truths... Whatever is known to us by consciousness is known beyond possibility of question... Logic has nothing to do with that portion of our knowledge."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In assessing arguments, recognize and set aside immediate-knowledge claims; restrict logical assessment to what is inferentially supported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to identify conditions that make facts prove other facts
rubrics_metrics.description: "Logic points out what relations must subsist between data and whatever can be concluded from them, between proof and every thing which it can prove."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proper evaluation checks whether necessary relations (e.g., causal relations, correlations under correct controls) between data and claimed conclusions are established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation and experiment as standards of induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple chapters and headings (Book III, Book IV) focus on "On Observation And Experiment," and Mill treats observation and experiment as central to inductive proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical claims must be supported by properly conducted observation and well-designed experiments; evaluate the adequacy of observational methods, controls, repeatability, and the experimental arrangement.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Four Methods of Experimental Inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Mill devotes a chapter to "Of The Four Methods Of Experimental Inquiry."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Mill's canonical experimental methods (the methods Mill formulates) as tools for causal inference in experimental contexts. These methods provide explicit tests for establishing causal connections from observed regularities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for causation and the law of universal causation
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapters include "Of Laws Of Nature," "Of The Law Of Universal Causation," and "On The Composition Of Causes."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing causal claims, examine whether evidence establishes causal laws, whether causes are composed or multiple, and whether the law of universal causation is a warranted assumption for the case at hand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling plurality and intermixture of causes and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Mill treats "Plurality Of Causes, And Of The Intermixture Of Effects" as a substantive problem for induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations must consider that observed effects may result from multiple interacting causes; isolate and test for intermixture to avoid confounding when inferring causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits to explanation and use of hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a chapter "Of The Limits To The Explanation Of Laws Of Nature; And Of Hypotheses."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors should recognize the legitimate limits of explanatory claims and how hypotheses are to be used (as provisional, not established proofs) — check whether hypotheses are empirically constrained and tested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of chance and probabilistic reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapters such as "Of Chance And Its Elimination" and "Of The Calculation Of Chances" treat how to handle chance in reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically examine how authors treat randomness and probability: whether chance has been eliminated appropriately, whether probabilistic calculations are applied correctly, and whether conclusions account for stochastic variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requisites of a philosophical language and principles of definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Book IV chapters include "Of The Requisites Of A Philosophical Language, And The Principles Of Definition."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good scientific and philosophical exposition must use well-defined, stable terms; evaluate definitions for clarity, avoidance of equivocation, and appropriateness for inductive purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification as subsidiary to induction, including classification by series
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapters "Of Classification, As Subsidiary To Induction" and "Of Classification By Series."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification schemes should aid detection of relevant resemblances and differences for induction; assess whether classifications are natural, useful for the inquiry, and do not obscure relevant causal patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification and avoidance of fallacies
rubrics_metrics.description: Book V is devoted to "On Fallacies" with chapters on classification of fallacies, fallacies of observation, generalization, ratiocination, confusion, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations must check for common fallacies (a priori fallacies, observational mistakes, over-generalization, false syllogisms, confusions) and hold arguments to criteria that guard against them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods appropriate to moral and social sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: Book VI treats "The Logic Of The Moral Sciences," discussing methods such as "The Chemical, Or Experimental, Method in the Social Science," "The Geometrical, Or Abstract, Method," "The Physical, Or Concrete Deductive, Method," and "The Inverse Deductive, Or Historical, Method."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating work in social or moral sciences, select and judge the appropriateness of method (experimental, abstract, deductive, historical) to the subject matter, recognizing limitations and special evidential problems in these fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation of laws of nature and extension to adjacent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapters include "Of The Explanation Of Laws Of Nature," "Of The Extension Of Derivative Laws To Adjacent Cases," and "Of Analogy."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether purported explanations of laws are convincing, whether derived laws are justifiably extended to adjacent cases, and whether analogical reasoning is used properly and supported by relevant similarities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical laws and the grounds of disbelief
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapters such as "Of Empirical Laws" and "Of The Grounds Of Disbelief" address criteria for accepting or rejecting empirical generalizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine the empirical basis for proposed laws, the degree of approximation, and the legitimate grounds for disbelieving claims (insufficient evidence, contradictory data, methodological flaws).
